claims.text: Increasing compositional disorder in single-phase high-entropy alloys induces local lattice distortions.
Disorder-induced local lattice distortions enhance electron-phonon coupling.
Enhanced electron-phonon coupling increases superconducting transition temperature relative to a lower-disorder baseline alloy.
Adding a minor alloying element increases atomic-scale chemical inhomogeneity.
Increased compositional disorder produces increased local lattice distortion.
Local lattice distortions modify the phonon spectrum.
Local lattice distortions modify the electronic density of states at the Fermi level.
The distortion-induced changes to phonons and the Fermi-level density of states enhance electron-phonon coupling.
Enhanced electron-phonon coupling promotes Cooper-pair formation.
More compositionally disordered alloys will have larger electron-phonon coupling parameters than lower-disorder alloys.
More compositionally disordered alloys will have higher superconducting transition temperatures than lower-disorder alloys while remaining single-phase.
A lower-disorder high-entropy-alloy baseline has smaller local lattice distortions.
A lower-disorder high-entropy-alloy baseline has a correspondingly lower superconducting transition temperature.
The proposed relationship is limited to a compositional range that avoids phase separation and significant structural instability.
Above some disorder threshold, extrinsic effects may dominate and the proposed disorder-superconductivity relationship may fail.
The magnitude and monotonicity of the transition-temperature response depend on alloy-system details and distortion extent.

contradictions.description: The intervention requires varying alloy composition by adding a minor element, whereas the experiment calls the samples identical in overall composition while also systematically varying the amount of introduced minor alloying element. Those requirements cannot both hold without an additional compensating-composition scheme, which is not specified.
